_note: STEM DEFECT (printed radical vinculum too wide) — transcribed AS PRINTED per the brief; RECOMMENDED REPAIR: denominator should be \(\sqrt{3x-11}-2\), i.e. change '\\sqrt{3x-11-2}' to '\\sqrt{3x-11}-2'. Evidence: (a) on the page the denominator's radical vinculum runs the full width of '3x-11-2' (verified at 10x zoom - two distinct horizontal rules, the upper being the fraction bar and the lower starting just after the radical tick and ending at the far right), whereas the NUMERATOR's vinculum in the same fraction correctly stops after '4' leaving '-3' outside; (b) the book CAN set a short vinculum in a denominator - Misc II Q17 prints \(\sqrt{2}-\sin x-\cos x\) correctly - so this is a defect, not house style; (c) AS PRINTED the denominator is \(\sqrt{3x-13}\), which at x=5 equals \(\sqrt{2}\ne 0\) while the numerator tends to 0, so the limit is 0 and NO option matches; (d) under the intended reading the 0/0 form rationalises to \((\sqrt{3x-11}+2)/(3(\sqrt{x+4}+3))\to 4/18 = 2/9\), exactly option D. My derived letter D is under the intended reading and matches the book's printed key.
solution: [Textbook misprint in the stem: the denominator's radical vinculum is set too wide, running over the whole of \(3x - 11 - 2\), so as printed the denominator reads \(\sqrt{3x-13}\). That reading makes the question unanswerable — at \(x = 5\) the denominator is \(\sqrt{2} \ne 0\) while the numerator tends to \(0\), giving a limit of \(0\), which is none of the four options. The intended denominator is \(\sqrt{3x-11} - 2\): the numerator's own vinculum in the same fraction correctly stops after the \(4\), leaving its \(-3\) outside, and the book sets a short denominator vinculum correctly elsewhere in this very exercise. Under the intended reading the \(0/0\) form rationalises to \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3x-11}+2}{3\left(\sqrt{x+4}+3\right)} \to \dfrac{4}{18} = \dfrac{2}{9}\), which is the printed key. The answer above follows the intended reading.]

solution: [Textbook defect in the OPTION SET, not in the key: options A and B are the SAME number written two ways, since \(\log 15 = \log(3 \times 5) = \log 3 + \log 5\). Both are distractors, so the key is unaffected — factoring the numerator as \(\left(3^x - 1\right)\left(5^x - 1\right)\) gives \(\log 3 \cdot \log 5\). Verified numerically: the quotient converges to \(1.768148\) from both sides, which is \(\log 3 \cdot \log 5\).]

_note: Printed exactly as 'secx^2 - 1' (italic 'secx' with a superscript 2 sitting on the x), i.e. \(\sec(x^{2})-1\), NOT \(\sec^{2}x-1\). Confirmed by the book's own key, which gives 1/2: \(\sec(x^{2})-1\sim x^{4}/2\) gives 1/2, whereas \(\sec^{2}x-1=\tan^{2}x\sim x^{2}\) over \(x^{4}\) would diverge. Transcribed as printed; the notation is ambiguous to a reader and could be worth an errata clarification.
solution: [Textbook notation, ambiguous as set: the numerator is printed with the \(2\) as a superscript on the \(x\) of an italic \(\sec x\), i.e. \(\sec\left(x^2\right) - 1\), NOT \(\sec^2 x - 1\). The book's own key settles it: \(\sec\left(x^2\right) - 1 \sim \frac{x^4}{2}\) gives the printed \(\frac{1}{2}\), whereas \(\sec^2 x - 1 = \tan^2 x \sim x^2\) over \(x^4\) would diverge. Read the argument as \(x^2\).]
